steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise overview of the main differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose sugar (lacks an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose sugar (has an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   – The extra hydroxyl in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  
   – Uracil pairs with adenine in RNA; thymine is methylated uracil.

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself to form short double-helical regions.  

4. Location in the cell  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA is confined to the nucleus (and organelles like mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cell—cytoplasm, ribosomes, and various organelles.  

5. Function  
   • DNA serves as the long-term repository of genetic information—essentially the blueprint for all proteins and regulatory elements.  
   • RNA has multiple roles, including:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries coded instructions from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids to ribosomes during protein synthesis.  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.  
     – Other regulatory and catalytic RNAs (e.g., miRNA, siRNA, ribozymes).

6. Stability and lifespan  
   • DNA is very stable, designed to last the life of a cell or organism.  
   • RNA is more transient—many RNA species have short half-lives so the cell can rapidly adjust protein production.

7. Synthesis and processing  
   • DNA replication copies the entire genome prior to cell division, using DNA polymerases.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA by RNA polymerases; it often undergoes processing (capping, splicing, polyadenylation in eukaryotes) before becoming mature mRNA.

8. Enzymatic machinery  
   • DNA uses DNA polymerases, helicases, ligases, topoisomerases, etc., for replication and repair.  
   • RNA synthesis and processing use RNA polymerases, spliceosomes, editing enzymes, etc.

Summary  
DNA is the stable, double-stranded molecule that stores genetic information, while RNA is a less stable, usually single-stranded molecule that plays diverse roles in translating that information into proteins and regulating gene expression.
